3350:
A consequence is something that happens because of something else. It is the result, the outcome, the "what follows" from an action, a decision, an event, or a situation.

The key idea baked into this word is cause and effect. Something happens first (the cause), and the consequence is what flows from it. You cannot have a consequence without something that caused it.

You didn't study. The consequence was that you failed the exam.

The failure didn't appear out of nowhere — it was directly produced by not studying. That link of "A caused B" is what makes B a consequence.
What makes "consequence" different from similar words

English has many words that seem to mean the same thing — result, effect, outcome, repercussion — and while they overlap, each carries a slightly different shade of meaning. Understanding where "consequence" sits among them will sharpen your feel for it.

Result is the most neutral and general of the group. It simply points to what came out of something, with no emotional weight at all.

The result of mixing blue and yellow is green.

Effect focuses on the impact something has, often in a more scientific or analytical sense. It emphasizes the influence one thing has on another.

The medicine had a calming effect on him.

Outcome feels more like the final destination — what a process, situation, or event ultimately leads to. It often carries a sense of conclusion.

The outcome of the negotiation was a peace agreement.

Consequence, by contrast, has a stronger sense of inevitability and weight. It often implies that what follows was earned — that an action or choice naturally brought about something. This is why you so often hear "consequence" in contexts involving responsibility, morality, decisions, and accountability. The word almost always carries the feeling that the result was meant to follow, whether as a logical conclusion or as a form of accountability.

There are serious consequences for breaking the law.

You would not normally say "there are serious outcomes for breaking the law" — it would sound flat, because "outcome" lacks that sense of earned weight.

Repercussion is closest to "consequence" in tone, but it leans specifically toward negative effects that ripple outward, often unexpectedly, like a shockwave from an initial action.

The scandal had repercussions across the entire organization.

"Consequence" is broader — it can be negative, positive, or neutral.
Consequences can be negative, positive, or neutral

This is important: the word itself does not judge. A consequence is simply what follows. Context and the situation around it determine whether it is good or bad.

Negative consequence:

He drove recklessly. The consequence was a serious accident.

Positive consequence:

She trained hard every day for a year. The consequence was that she won the championship.

Neutral consequence:

They moved to a new city. One consequence was that they had to find new schools for their children.

In everyday speech, however, people often use "consequences" to mean specifically negative ones — especially when warning someone. "You'll face the consequences" almost always means something bad is coming. But the word itself is technically neutral, and in formal writing it is used for any kind of result.

One of the most important textures of the word "consequence" is that it implies the result was unavoidable — it had to follow from what came before. This is what gives the word its gravity and seriousness.

When someone says, "Your actions have consequences," they are not just saying "things happen." They are saying: what you do determines what comes back to you. There is a kind of natural law being invoked — choices lead to outcomes, and you cannot escape that chain.

This is why the word is used so often in moral, legal, and professional contexts, where accountability matters.

Consequences can be small or large, immediate or delayed, personal or wide-reaching.

  • A small, immediate, personal consequence: You forget your umbrella; the consequence is you get wet.
  • A large, delayed, wide-reaching consequence: A government raises interest rates; the consequence is that millions of people find it harder to borrow money over the next two years.

The word works equally well at all these scales.

"As a consequence" — this phrase is used to signal that what you are about to say was caused by something just mentioned. It is slightly more formal than "so" or "therefore."

The factory was shut down. As a consequence, hundreds of workers lost their jobs.

"In consequence" — very similar to "as a consequence," and slightly more formal.

The bridge was damaged in the flood. In consequence, the road was closed for three weeks.

"Face the consequences" — to accept or endure the bad results of something you did.

He lied to his employer. Now he must face the consequences.

"Suffer the consequences" — similar to "face the consequences," but with emphasis on the pain or difficulty involved.

"Have consequences" — a phrase used to warn that something will not go unpunished or without effect.

Your decision will have serious consequences.

"Without consequences" — meaning without any penalty or harmful result. Often used to describe situations that feel unfairly free of accountability.

He walked away from the crash without consequences.
The second meaning: importance or significance

This is a less common but legitimate meaning of "consequence," mostly found in formal writing and older literature.

In this sense, "consequence" means importance, significance, or weight.

It is a matter of no consequence. (= It does not matter; it is unimportant.)
She is a person of great consequence in the industry. (= She is an important, influential person.)

You will mostly encounter this meaning in formal contexts, classic literature, or phrases like "of little consequence" and "of no consequence." In modern everyday speech, people more commonly say "of no importance" or "it doesn't matter," but knowing this meaning ensures you won't be confused when you encounter it.

"Consequence" is a word about the chain between actions and what follows from them. It asks you to think about how the present moment was shaped by past choices, and how today's choices will shape tomorrow. It carries a sense of weight — that things are connected, that nothing happens in a vacuum, and that what you do matters and leaves a mark.

When you see or hear "consequence," ask yourself: What came before that caused this? The answer to that question is always the heart of what the word is pointing to.
3351:
Consequent means following as a direct result of something. If one thing causes another, the second thing is consequent — it is the outcome that flows naturally from the first.

The key idea inside this word is a causal chain: not just "this came after that," but "this came because of that." There is always a cause-and-effect relationship hiding inside "consequent."

The most common pattern in formal or written English is:

consequent on something, or consequent upon something

Here are clear examples:

  • "The factory closed, and the consequent job losses devastated the town."
    The job losses happened because of the closure. They are consequent upon it.
  • "There was a sharp rise in prices, consequent on the fuel shortage."
    The price rise was a direct result of the fuel shortage.
  • "The flooding and the consequent damage to infrastructure cost millions."
    First the flood, then the damage — and the damage exists because the flood happened.

You can also use "consequent" without "on/upon" when the cause is already clear from context:

  • "The disease spread quickly, causing consequent panic across the region."
    "Consequent" here points back at the spread of disease as the cause.

In every case, ask yourself: "Is there a clear cause that produced this result?" If yes, "consequent" fits.
The Most Important Distinction: Consequent vs. Consequential

This is where almost everyone goes wrong, and getting this right will put you ahead of most people.

Consequent = something that follows from a cause. It looks backward at what produced it.

Consequential = something that is important, significant, or impactful. It looks forward at the effects it will have on the world.

Read these two sentences carefully:

"The war and its consequent suffering."
"The war was the most consequential event of the century."

In the first sentence, "consequent suffering" means the suffering that resulted from the war — the war is the cause, the suffering is the outcome.

In the second sentence, "consequential event" means the war was enormously important and far-reaching — it shaped everything that came after it.

So "consequent" is never about importance or significance on its own. If someone says a decision was "consequent," they are not calling it important — they are saying it followed from something. If they want to call it important, the right word is "consequential."

A simple test: can you replace the word with "resulting from" or "following from"? If yes → consequent. Can you replace it with "important" or "significant"? If yes → consequential.
Another Key Distinction: Consequent vs. Subsequent

These two are also commonly mixed up.

Subsequent simply means coming later in time. It has no causal meaning — it just says something happened after something else, with no claim about why.

Consequent means coming later in time AND because of the first thing. Causation is built in.

"The rain fell, and the subsequent sunshine dried everything out."
→ The sunshine just came after the rain, not because of it. No causal link.

"The drought and the consequent famine."
→ The famine happened because of the drought. Clear causal link.

If you could reasonably say "this happened after, but not necessarily because of," use subsequent. If the cause-and-effect link is real and direct, use consequent.
A Special Use: Consequent in Logic

In formal logic, "consequent" has a precise technical meaning. A logical statement often takes this form:

"If P, then Q."

Here, P is called the antecedent (the "if" part), and Q is called the consequent (the "then" part). The consequent is the outcome that follows if the condition is satisfied.

For example: "If it rains, the ground gets wet."
— The consequent is "the ground gets wet" — it is what follows from the condition being true.

This is a more technical use, but it rests on the exact same core idea: the consequent is what logically follows from what came before.
A Quick Mental Model to Remember It

Imagine a row of dominoes falling. The first domino tips over and knocks the next one down. The second domino falling is consequent — it happened because of the first. The chain of falling dominoes is a chain of consequent events, each one caused by the one before.

"Consequent" always signals: there is something behind this that caused it.

"Consequent" describes something that directly follows from a cause. It carries a built-in cause-and-effect relationship. It is used most naturally in the patterns consequent on or consequent upon something, or as an attributive adjective when the cause is clear from context. It is not a synonym for "important" (that would be consequential), and it is not a synonym for "coming after in time" alone (that would be subsequent). It always answers the question: "What came out of that cause?"
3352:
"Consequential" describes something that produces significant consequences — meaning it matters a lot, it carries real weight, and its effects ripple forward and change things in a meaningful way.

Think of it this way: if something is "consequential," it doesn't just exist quietly. It does something. It affects things. It leaves a mark.

This word has two distinct meanings — one that is very common today, and one that is old-fashioned and rare.

Meaning 1 — Important and impactful (the main, modern meaning)

This is the meaning you will almost always encounter. Something is "consequential" when it is significant enough to have a real, lasting effect on people, events, or outcomes.

Examples:

  • "Choosing a career is one of the most consequential decisions a person makes."

→ This choice will shape your entire life. It matters enormously.

  • "The election was highly consequential for the future of the country."

→ The result of this election will lead to major changes that affect many people.

  • "Einstein was one of the most consequential scientists in history."

→ His work didn't just exist — it fundamentally changed how humanity understands the universe.

  • "That was a consequential mistake."

→ This wasn't a small, forgettable error. It caused serious downstream problems.

  • "The meeting lasted only 20 minutes, but it was deeply consequential."

→ Despite being short, what was decided in that room changed everything that followed.

Notice the pattern: "consequential" always points to impact and reach. It's not just about something being notable or interesting — it's about something having real consequences that ripple outward.

Meaning 2 — Pompous or self-important (rare, old-fashioned)

In older or more literary writing, "consequential" can describe a person who acts as if they are very important — often when they are not. It is a slightly mocking description of someone full of themselves.

Example:

  • "He walked into the room with a consequential air, as though everyone should stop and take notice of him."

→ He was putting on airs of importance and significance.

This meaning is uncommon in modern everyday language. You might encounter it in 18th or 19th century literature, but in contemporary writing and speech, Meaning 1 dominates almost entirely. If you use the word, assume people will read it as Meaning 1.

One important nuance: "consequential" isn't a simple synonym for "important." It specifically highlights that something generates effects — that it has downstream influence.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "This is an important document." → You're saying it deserves attention or respect.
  • "This is a consequential document." → You're saying this document will change things. Something will be different because of it.

The word carries a sense of cause and effect. A consequential event is one that sets other things into motion.

This is also why "consequential" often implies seriousness and weight. When someone calls a decision "consequential," they are usually signaling that it should not be taken lightly, because the stakes are high and the effects will be real and lasting.

The clearest way to anchor a word is to know its opposite. The opposite of "consequential" is inconsequential — meaning something that has no significant effect, something trivial or unimportant.

  • "Don't worry about it — it's a completely inconsequential detail."

→ It doesn't matter. It won't change anything.

  • "His role in the project was inconsequential."

→ He was barely involved, and his contribution made no real difference.

Thinking of these two words as a scale helps: the more consequential something is, the more it matters and the more it affects the world around it. The more inconsequential, the less it matters at all.
Words That Often Appear Alongside It

In real usage, "consequential" is commonly paired with words that emphasize scale and impact:

  • Highly consequential — used to stress just how significant something is
  • Most consequential — often used to rank impact ("the most consequential moment of the century")
  • Deeply consequential — emphasizes emotional or lasting weight
  • Potentially consequential — used when the full impact is not yet known

And it frequently appears with nouns like: decision, choice, moment, election, policy, era, figure, mistake, agreement, action.

"Consequential" is a slightly formal word. You'll see it often in journalism, politics, history, law, and academic writing. It's perfectly natural in thoughtful conversation too, but you'd be less likely to hear it in casual small talk.

It is not a word that whispers. When someone calls something "consequential," they are signaling gravity and seriousness. It gives weight to whatever it describes.

Do not confuse "consequential" with "consequent" (a different adjective). "Consequent" simply means "following as a result of something" ("the flood and the consequent damage"). It is more neutral and mechanical — it just says that B followed from A. "Consequential," by contrast, carries the added meaning of significance and impact. Something can be consequent without being consequential (a small, trivial result that followed from something), but if something is truly consequential, it is both a result and a significant one.

Consequential = producing significant, meaningful consequences; important in a way that genuinely affects and changes things.

If something is consequential, it matters — not just on the surface, but in a way that sends ripples forward. It is a word about impact, weight, and real-world effect.
3353:
Consequently means "as a result of that" or "because of what just happened."

When you use consequently, you are telling your reader or listener: "Here is what happened. Now, because of that, this next thing also happened." It is a word that connects a cause to its effect.

Think of it as a signpost. It points backwards (to a reason or situation) and then points forward (to the result that came out of it).

Every time you use consequently, you are saying two things at once:

  1. Something happened or is true.
  2. Because of that thing, something else followed.

The word sits between those two facts and acts as the bridge.

The road was icy. Consequently, many drivers slowed down.

Here, "many drivers slowed down" is the direct result of the road being icy. Consequently makes that connection clear and explicit.
How It Sits in a Sentence

Consequently most often appears at the beginning of a new sentence or after a semicolon, introducing the result clause. It is almost always followed by a comma.

Pattern 1 — Two separate sentences:

She did not study for the exam. Consequently, she failed.

Pattern 2 — Two clauses joined by a semicolon:

She did not study for the exam; consequently, she failed.

You will occasionally see it mid-sentence as well, though this is less common:

She failed the exam, consequently losing her scholarship.
The Relationship It Expresses: Cause → Effect

This is the heart of the word. Consequently always signals direct consequence — that is, the result is not accidental or coincidental. It flows logically and directly from the cause.

Ask yourself: "Did the first thing genuinely lead to the second thing?" If yes, consequently fits perfectly.

The company spent more than it earned for years. Consequently, it went bankrupt.

The bankruptcy was not a random event. It happened because of the overspending. That direct logical link is exactly what consequently expresses.

Let's see it in many different kinds of situations so the pattern becomes second nature.

Health:

He never exercised and ate poorly. Consequently, his health declined rapidly by middle age.

Weather and events:

The storm knocked out the power grid. Consequently, the entire city was in darkness for two days.

Work and decisions:

The manager ignored every warning from the team. Consequently, the project failed completely.

Science and nature:

The river was dammed upstream. Consequently, the fish population downstream collapsed.

Everyday life:

She missed the last train. Consequently, she had to walk home in the rain.

Law and rules:

He broke the terms of his contract. Consequently, he was taken to court.

Learning:

The students practised writing every day. Consequently, their skills improved dramatically.

In every single example, notice: the first sentence is the cause, and the sentence beginning with consequently is the effect.

Consequently is a formal and neutral word. You will find it in:

  • Academic writing (essays, research papers)
  • Professional writing (reports, business emails)
  • News articles and journalism
  • Formal speeches

It sounds slightly stiff in casual everyday conversation. If you are texting a friend, you would more naturally say "so":

  • Casual: "I missed the bus, so I was late."
  • Formal: "I missed the bus. Consequently, I arrived late."

Both are correct. Consequently simply carries more weight and precision.
How It Compares to Similar Words

You will often see words used alongside consequently or in its place. Here is how they differ:

So — the most casual option; same meaning but used in everyday speech and writing.

It rained, so we stayed inside.

Therefore — very close to consequently; also formal, but often used more in logical arguments and reasoning (maths, philosophy, debates).

All humans are mortal. Socrates is human. Therefore, Socrates is mortal.

Thus — similar to therefore; slightly more old-fashioned and formal; often used in academic or literary writing.

The evidence was weak; thus, the case was dismissed.

Hence — also formal; often used in academic or technical writing; slightly more emphatic.

The data was incomplete; hence, no conclusion could be drawn.

As a result — almost identical in meaning to consequently; slightly less formal and very natural in both speech and writing.

The bridge was damaged. As a result, traffic was diverted.

The key difference is subtle: consequently tends to stress that the outcome was a natural, direct, and logical follow-on — almost inevitable given the cause. Therefore is more often used when you are making a reasoned conclusion. But in most everyday writing, consequently, therefore, and as a result can be used interchangeably.

Do not use consequently to connect two things that are merely related but where one did not cause the other.

❌ It rained yesterday. Consequently, I love the colour blue.
(Rain did not cause your love of blue. There is no cause-and-effect here. This is wrong.)

✅ It rained yesterday. Consequently, the ground is wet today.
(The rain directly caused the wet ground. This is correct.)

Always ask yourself: "Did the first thing genuinely produce or cause the second thing?" If the answer is no, consequently is the wrong word.
"Consequently" is an adverb that means "as a direct result of that" — it connects a cause to its effect, telling your audience that what follows happened because of what was just stated.
3354:
Conservation is the careful protection of something valuable so that it is not lost, wasted, damaged, or destroyed — either for the benefit of people alive today, or for future generations, or both.

Conservation is about keeping something intact or functional by managing it wisely. It is not the same as locking something away and never touching it. It means using something responsibly, or protecting it actively, so it continues to exist and remain useful.

The word has two broad meanings depending on the context — one used in everyday life and one used in science.

1. The Everyday/Practical Sense: Protection and Careful Management

This is the most common use. Conservation here means taking deliberate steps to protect a resource, a species, a place, or a thing from being damaged, overused, or wiped out.

A. Nature and Wildlife Conservation
This is probably the first thing most people think of. When people work to protect endangered animals, forests, rivers, coral reefs, or entire ecosystems, that is conservation. For example, efforts to stop tigers from going extinct — breeding programs, protecting forest habitats, banning hunting — are all forms of wildlife conservation.

The idea is that nature has value and that human activity (hunting, pollution, deforestation, development) can destroy it faster than it can recover. Conservation is the act of slowing or stopping that destruction.

B. Environmental Conservation
Broader than just wildlife, this includes protecting the air, water, soil, and climate from damage. Reducing pollution, controlling industrial waste, protecting wetlands, and managing national parks all fall under environmental conservation.

C. Energy Conservation
This means using less energy — not wasting it. Turning off lights when you leave a room, using energy-efficient appliances, insulating your home so heat doesn't escape — all of these are acts of energy conservation. The goal is to reduce unnecessary consumption so that energy resources (and the environment) are not depleted faster than necessary.

D. Water Conservation
Using water wisely so it is not wasted. Fixing leaky pipes, taking shorter showers, using drip irrigation in farming rather than flooding fields — these are all water conservation practices. This matters especially in areas that face drought or scarcity.

E. Conservation of Art, History, and Culture
This sense refers to preserving things made by humans — paintings, sculptures, old buildings, ancient manuscripts, archaeological sites, and cultural traditions. A museum conservator, for example, repairs a 500-year-old painting so it does not deteriorate. Restoring a historic building so it doesn't crumble is also conservation. Here, the goal is to prevent time, neglect, or environmental damage from erasing our shared human heritage.

2. The Scientific Sense: A Principle of Physics and Chemistry

In science, conservation has a more technical and precise meaning. It refers to a fundamental law or principle stating that a particular quantity in a closed system remains constant — it does not increase or decrease, no matter what happens inside the system.

The most famous examples:

  • Conservation of Energy: Energy cannot be created from nothing, nor can it be destroyed. It can only change from one form to another. When you burn fuel in an engine, chemical energy converts to heat and motion, but the total amount of energy in the system stays the same. Nothing is gained; nothing disappears.
  • Conservation of Mass: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the substances before the reaction equals the total mass after. Atoms are just rearranged, not created or destroyed.
  • Conservation of Momentum: In a collision between objects, the total momentum of the system before the collision equals the total momentum after it (assuming no outside forces act on the system).

In this scientific sense, conservation does not require any human effort or intention. It is simply a law of nature — a description of how the universe behaves. Scientists discovered that certain quantities are always "conserved," meaning they remain unchanged through a process.

These two words are often confused, so it is worth understanding the difference clearly.

  • Conservation accepts that humans will interact with nature or resources, but insists that this be done carefully and sustainably. A conservation forest, for example, may allow logging — but only a limited amount, done in ways that allow the forest to recover.
  • Preservation means keeping something completely untouched and unchanged, with no human use or interference at all. A preserved wilderness area allows no logging, no farming, no development whatsoever.

So conservation is about wise and managed use, while preservation is about no use at all. Both are valid approaches, but they have different goals and are applied in different situations.
The Underlying Theme Across All Uses

Whether you are talking about forests, energy, a Renaissance painting, or the momentum of billiard balls, the word conservation always carries the same underlying idea:

Something of value exists. There is a risk it could be lost or wasted. Conservation is the act — or the principle — that keeps it from being lost.

In human contexts (environment, energy, art), this requires conscious effort and deliberate choices. In scientific contexts, it is a law that nature follows automatically.
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "The conservation of rainforests is essential to maintaining biodiversity."
  • "She practiced water conservation by collecting rainwater for her garden."
  • "The museum's conservation department carefully restored the ancient scroll."
  • "The law of conservation of energy is one of the most fundamental principles in physics."
  • "The government set aside large areas of land for wildlife conservation."
  • "Energy conservation at home can significantly reduce your electricity bills."

Conservation, as a noun, refers either to the active protection and careful management of something valuable — such as nature, energy, water, or cultural heritage — so that it is not lost, wasted, or destroyed; or to a fundamental scientific principle stating that a certain quantity (like energy or mass) remains constant and unchanged within a system. The unifying idea is always the same: something important is kept from being lost.
3355:
A conservative is a person who believes in preserving what already exists — existing traditions, institutions, values, and ways of doing things — and who is cautious, even skeptical, about rapid or sweeping change.

The word comes from the idea of conserving (keeping, protecting). So a conservative is someone who says: "What we have has worked. Let's not throw it away too quickly."
Where You'll Most Often Hear It

The noun "a conservative" is used almost exclusively in political and social contexts. It describes a person's ideology — their set of beliefs about how society should be organized and governed.

Example sentences:

  • "She is a conservative who opposes higher taxes."
  • "Conservatives in the Senate blocked the new bill."
  • "He has always been a conservative — he dislikes sudden change."

Conservatives don't all believe exactly the same things, but most share a common set of values:

1. Tradition matters.
Conservatives believe that traditions, customs, and social institutions — like family, religion, and law — have been tested by time and have survived because they work. They are not to be discarded lightly just because someone has a new idea.

2. Change should be slow and careful.
A conservative doesn't necessarily oppose all change. They oppose fast, radical, or untested change. They prefer gradual reform — changing things step by step, making sure each step is stable before taking the next.

3. Limited government.
Most conservatives believe government should stay out of people's lives as much as possible. They think individuals, families, and local communities are better at solving problems than large, centralized governments.

4. Personal responsibility.
Conservatives tend to believe that individuals should take care of themselves and their families, rather than depending on the state. If you face a problem, the answer is usually your own effort, your family, or your community — not a government program.

5. Free markets.
Economically, conservatives typically believe that the economy works best when businesses and individuals make their own decisions freely, with minimal government interference. They often support lower taxes and less regulation.

6. Order and stability.
Conservatives value social order — they believe a stable, law-abiding society is essential before anything else can flourish. This is why they tend to strongly support law enforcement, the military, and national security.

The word is broad enough that there are several kinds of conservatives. Knowing these helps you understand the word more fully:

Fiscal conservative — primarily concerned with money and the economy. Believes in cutting government spending, reducing debt, and keeping taxes low. Might not care as much about social or cultural issues.

Social conservative — primarily concerned with preserving traditional moral and cultural values. Typically holds conventional views on marriage, family structure, gender roles, and religion.

National conservative — places strong emphasis on national identity, sovereignty, border control, and putting one's own country's interests first. Skeptical of globalism and international organizations.

Paleoconservative — an older, more traditionalist strand. Very cautious about foreign military involvement, strongly protective of cultural heritage, and skeptical of mass immigration.

Neoconservative — believes in using American or Western power (including military force) to spread democracy and liberal values abroad, while still holding conservative domestic views. More internationally interventionist than other conservatives.

Libertarian-leaning conservative — emphasizes individual freedom above nearly everything else. Wants the government out of both the economy and personal life.

In practice, most conservatives are a mix of these. A person might be a fiscal conservative but a social moderate, or a national conservative who also holds libertarian economic views.

This distinction is important:

Lowercase "conservative" → refers to an ideology or a general disposition. Anyone who believes in the conservative philosophy.

  • "My grandfather is a conservative — he hates unnecessary change."

Uppercase "Conservative" → refers to a member or supporter of a specific political party that calls itself the Conservative Party. This is most common in countries like the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, which have official parties with that name.

  • "She voted Conservative in the last election." (UK context)
  • "He's a Conservative MP." (Member of Parliament, UK)

In the United States, the major right-leaning party is the Republican Party, not the Conservative Party — so Americans use the lowercase "conservative" for the ideology and "Republican" for the party.
How a Conservative Differs from Similar Terms

Conservative vs. Liberal
These are classic opposites in politics. A liberal welcomes change, believes in expanding individual rights, supports a larger role for government in reducing inequality, and is more open to new social norms. A conservative prefers stability, tradition, and limited government. In everyday speech, these are the two most common ideological labels in English.

Conservative vs. Progressive
A progressive actively pushes for social, economic, and political change — often significant and fast-moving. A conservative resists this. Where a progressive says "Things need to change now," a conservative says "Not so fast."

Conservative vs. Reactionary
A reactionary doesn't just want to preserve the present — they want to reverse change and go back to the past. A conservative wants to keep what exists; a reactionary wants to undo what has already changed. "Reactionary" is generally considered a more extreme label.

Conservative vs. Moderate
A moderate sits somewhere between conservative and liberal, not fully committed to either side. A conservative has a clear ideological direction.
The Word in Everyday, Non-Political Use

Though rare in pure noun form outside of politics, you may sometimes hear it used informally:

  • "On financial matters, she's a conservative."

Here it means she's cautious, careful, and doesn't take big risks with money. The spirit of the word is the same — preference for caution over boldness — just applied outside of politics.

A conservative is a person who values tradition, distrusts rapid change, and believes that individuals, families, and free markets — rather than large governments — are the best foundations for a stable and prosperous society.
3356: A conservatoire is a specialist school or college dedicated to training students in the performing arts — most commonly music, but sometimes also dance, drama, or opera — at a professional level.

Think of it this way: a regular university teaches many subjects (history, science, languages, etc.) and might have a music department as one of many. A conservatoire is the opposite — it exists solely to produce professional performing artists. Every classroom, every teacher, every timetable, everything is organized around one purpose: turning talented students into performance-ready professionals.

A student at a conservatoire doesn't study biology or economics. They spend their days practising their instrument for hours, taking lessons with expert tutors, performing in ensembles and orchestras, studying music theory and history, and learning the craft of being a performer from every possible angle. It is intense, focused, and demanding.

Conservatoires are for people who are already seriously skilled and want to pursue a career in performance. You don't go to a conservatoire to discover whether you like music — you go because you have already spent years developing your ability and you are committed to making it your profession. Entry is highly competitive and almost always requires an audition, not just academic qualifications.

Students can be at undergraduate level (typically 18+ year-olds after school) or postgraduate level (those who have already completed a degree and want to specialize further). Some conservatoires also have junior programs for younger, exceptionally gifted students who attend alongside their regular schooling.
What makes it different from a music school or music college

The word "music school" can mean almost anything — a local school where children learn piano, a weekend class, or a small community program. A conservatoire is something far more specific and elevated. It is a higher education institution, recognized at the same level as a university, that awards proper degrees and diplomas. The training is at the highest professional standard, often taught by performers who are themselves active in the profession.

A music college is broadly similar in purpose, but in practice, "conservatoire" is a title associated with institutions that have a particular prestige, history, and standard of training. Not every music college calls itself a conservatoire — it is a name that carries weight and implies a serious, rigorous environment.

While performance is always at the heart of a conservatoire, students study a range of supporting subjects:

  • Individual performance lessons — one-on-one tuition with a specialist teacher in your instrument or voice
  • Ensemble and orchestral playing — performing together in groups of all sizes
  • Music theory and harmony — understanding the technical structure of music
  • Aural training — developing the ear to recognize and reproduce musical ideas
  • Music history and literature — understanding the context and tradition of what you are performing
  • Conducting, composition, or music technology — depending on the conservatoire and the course

The balance shifts heavily toward the practical rather than the academic. A conservatoire student spends far more time performing and practising than writing essays.

Most conservatoires focus on classical music, but the term can apply to institutions specializing in:

  • Classical and orchestral music — the most common type
  • Jazz — some institutions specialize specifically in jazz performance
  • Opera — some have dedicated opera schools or programs
  • Drama and theatre — some conservatoires teach acting at a high professional level
  • Dance — specialist institutions training professional ballet or contemporary dancers
  • Combined performing arts — some teach music, dance, and drama together under one roof

These two words mean exactly the same thing. "Conservatoire" is the spelling used in British English (borrowed directly from the French), while "conservatory" is the American English equivalent. If you are reading a British or European text, you will see "conservatoire." In American contexts, you will more often see "conservatory." Both refer to the same kind of institution.

(Be careful: in British English, "conservatory" can also mean something completely different — a glass-roofed room attached to a house for sitting in. That is an entirely separate meaning. When talking about music and the arts, "conservatoire" removes that ambiguity.)

To help you picture what these institutions actually look like in the real world, some well-known examples include:

  • The Royal Academy of Music (London) — one of the oldest and most prestigious in the world
  • The Royal College of Music (London)
  • The Paris Conservatoire (France) — historically one of the most influential music institutions in the world
  • The Royal Conservatoire of Scotland (Glasgow)
  • The Guildhall School of Music & Drama (London) — covers both music and drama
  • The Juilliard School (New York) — the American equivalent, called a conservatory

Life at a conservatoire is defined by discipline, competition, and artistic ambition. Students are surrounded by peers who are equally or more talented than them, which can be both inspiring and humbling. Practising for many hours a day is normal. There are regular performances, assessments, and masterclasses where students perform in front of expert visitors from the profession. The environment is designed to simulate the pressures of a professional career.

There is also a strong sense of community and tradition. Students often form ensembles, chamber groups, or bands with their peers. The social life tends to revolve around music itself. Many lifelong professional partnerships and friendships are formed at conservatoires.

A conservatoire is a specialist higher-education institution dedicated to training students to become professional performing artists — most commonly musicians. It is not a general university with a music department; it is a place where everything is oriented toward one goal: producing excellent performers. Entry is competitive, training is intensive, and the environment is one of serious artistic purpose. The word is used mainly in British and European contexts; the American English equivalent is "conservatory."
3357: The word conservatory (noun) has two distinct meanings. Both are in common use today, and which one is meant depends entirely on context.
Meaning 1: A School for Music (or Performing Arts)

A conservatory is a specialized school where students are trained to a very high professional level in music, and sometimes in other performing arts like dance or drama.

Think of it this way: a regular school teaches many subjects. A university music department teaches music alongside other things. But a conservatory is entirely devoted to training serious, advanced musicians. It is intense, focused, and professional in nature. Students there are not casual learners — they are typically training to become professional performers, composers, or conductors.

What makes a conservatory different from an ordinary music school?

The key difference is the level of seriousness and the depth of training. A conservatory operates much like a university — it grants degrees — but every course, every hour of instruction, is centered around mastering music at the highest possible level. Students spend many hours a day practicing their instruments or voice. Lessons, rehearsals, performances, theory classes, and ear training fill their entire schedule. A student at a conservatory is, in a sense, already being treated as a professional-in-training.

Examples:

  • The Royal Conservatory of Music in Toronto, Canada.
  • The New England Conservatory in Boston, USA.
  • The Paris Conservatoire in France (this is the French spelling of the same word, used for French institutions).

You will often see the word shortened in conversation: "She studied at a conservatory" or "He graduated from the conservatory." This usage is most common in the context of classical music, though some conservatories also train students in jazz, opera, or musical theatre.
Meaning 2: A Glass Room Attached to a House

A conservatory is also a room with large glass walls and often a glass roof, built onto the side of a house, typically used as a bright, sunny sitting area or for growing plants.

Picture a regular living room. Now imagine replacing most of its walls and ceiling with glass panels. Light floods in from all sides. You can look out at the garden while sitting inside, sheltered from rain and cold. That is a conservatory.

Why glass? Because the original purpose was to conserve — meaning to keep alive and protect — delicate plants that could not survive outdoors during cold weather. The glass lets in sunlight while keeping out frost and wind. Over time, however, conservatories became fashionable as comfortable, light-filled living spaces, and many modern conservatories are used mainly as lounges, dining areas, or home offices rather than plant rooms.

How is a conservatory different from a greenhouse?

A greenhouse is a structure entirely built for growing plants — it is rarely used as a living space for people, and it is usually a standalone building in a garden. A conservatory, by contrast, is attached directly to the house and is designed to be lived in comfortably by people. It has proper flooring, furniture, heating, and décor. Growing plants in it is optional, not the main purpose.

This meaning of the word is especially common in British English. In the UK, adding a conservatory to the back of a house is a very popular home improvement project. In American English, a similar structure might instead be called a sunroom or sun porch.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Meant

Context makes it clear almost immediately:

  • If someone says, "She got accepted to the conservatory and will be studying violin," — it's the music school.
  • If someone says, "We had tea in the conservatory overlooking the garden," — it's the glass room.

There is no overlap between these two meanings. They are simply two separate things that share the same word.
A Note on Register and Tone

Both meanings carry a certain sense of refinement and prestige. A conservatory (music school) is not just any music class — it suggests elite, serious training. A conservatory (glass room) is not just any extension — it suggests a graceful, light-filled space. The word itself, in both uses, tends to appear in contexts that feel somewhat elevated or formal.

Music conservatoryA top-level school dedicated entirely to training professional musicians (or performing artists).
Home conservatoryA glass-walled room attached to a house, used as a bright living space or for growing plants.
3358: To conserve something means to protect it from being wasted, lost, or destroyed — by using it carefully or by actively working to keep it safe and available. The word holds two closely linked ideas at the same time: don't waste it, and make sure it lasts. Both ideas are almost always present when this word is used.
Why it's different from just "leaving something alone"

Conserving is an active, deliberate effort — not passivity. When you conserve something, you are consciously choosing to handle it with care because you recognize it is valuable, limited, or at risk. If nothing were done, it could run out, be damaged, or disappear entirely. That awareness of risk — and the intentional action taken against it — is at the heart of this word.

In day-to-day usage, people conserve things like water, electricity, fuel, and even their own physical energy. If a region is going through a drought, people are told to conserve water — meaning they should use only what is truly necessary and avoid any waste. If your phone battery is critically low, you might conserve battery life by switching off features you don't currently need. The logic is always the same: a limited resource is at risk of running out, so you use it wisely.

This is probably the most common context in which you'll encounter the word. Organisations around the world work to conserve endangered species (animals and plants that are close to extinction), conserve forests, conserve coral reefs, and conserve natural habitats. Here, the meaning leans more toward protecting from destruction than just careful use — because once a species goes extinct or a forest is cleared, it cannot simply be brought back. The stakes are permanent, which is why the word carries a sense of urgency in this context.
For a person's physical or mental strength

You can also conserve your own energy or strength. A long-distance runner might conserve her energy in the early miles of a race, deliberately holding back, so she has enough left to sprint at the finish. A doctor might advise a recovering patient to conserve their strength by resting instead of overexerting themselves. In this sense, the "resource" being carefully managed is the person's own body or stamina.

In physics and chemistry, conserve has a precise and important technical meaning. It means that a particular quantity remains exactly constant throughout a process — it does not increase, and it does not decrease. The famous Law of Conservation of Energy, for example, states that energy is never created from nothing and never destroyed — it only changes from one form to another (like heat turning into motion), but the total amount is always conserved. This scientific usage is more rigid and mathematical than the everyday usage, but the underlying spirit is the same: the thing in question doesn't get lost.

Conserve is also used when talking about protecting human-made things of historical or cultural value — ancient paintings, old manuscripts, archaeological artifacts, historic buildings. When a specialist conserves a centuries-old painting, they work carefully to stop further decay and stabilise it so that future generations can still experience it. This usage overlaps heavily with the word "restore," though conserving focuses more on halting damage, while restoring focuses on returning something to an earlier state.
How it compares to similar words

Save is broader and more general — you save something in the moment, from immediate danger. Conserve implies a sustained, ongoing, careful effort rather than a single rescue act.

Preserve is the closest synonym and often interchangeable. However, preserve tends to emphasise keeping something exactly as it is (like preserving food so it doesn't spoil, or preserving a historical site so it stays unchanged). Conserve tends to be preferred when talking about resources and the natural world, and it more strongly carries the idea of careful use to prevent depletion.

Protect means to shield something from harm. Conserve adds something extra — not just shielding, but also not squandering or exhausting a limited supply.

Maintain means to keep something in good working condition. Conserve carries the additional idea that the supply is finite and could be exhausted, which maintain does not.

"We need to conserve water during the dry season." — "The marathon runner conserved her energy in the first half and gave everything in the final kilometre." — "Scientists are working urgently to conserve the snow leopard's natural habitat." — "Switching off lights when you leave a room helps conserve electricity." — "The museum employs specialists who conserve ancient artifacts for future generations." — "According to the laws of physics, momentum is conserved in a closed system."

To conserve something is to treat it with careful, deliberate respect — using it wisely, protecting it from harm, and making sure it is not wasted or lost — because it is valuable and, often, limited.
3359: Consider means to think carefully and deliberately about something. The key word is carefully — "consider" is not a quick, passing thought. It implies giving something real mental attention, turning it over in your mind before you decide, judge, or act.

"Consider" has three closely related but distinct senses. Understanding all three will give you complete command of the word.

Meaning 1 — To think carefully about something (especially before deciding)

This is the most fundamental meaning. When you consider something, you are pausing to give it serious thought — weighing your options, examining the facts, looking at something from different angles.

Examples:

  • "Please consider my proposal before saying no."
  • "She considered her options for a long time before deciding."
  • "Have you considered what might go wrong?"
  • "Take a moment to consider the risks."

Notice the implication: you haven't decided yet. You're still in the process of thinking. This sense of "consider" often appears just before a decision is made.

Meaning 2 — To regard or view someone/something in a particular way (to hold an opinion)

In this sense, "consider" expresses a belief or judgment about something. It means: "In my opinion, X is Y." or "I view X as Y."

Sentence pattern: consider + person/thing + what you think of them

Examples:

  • "I consider him one of the best writers alive." (= I view him as one of the best)
  • "They consider this behavior unacceptable." (= They view this behavior as unacceptable)
  • "She considers honesty the most important quality in a person."
  • "Do you consider yourself an expert?"
  • "The judge considered the evidence sufficient."

This is different from Meaning 1. Here, you are not still thinking — you have already reached a view, and you are expressing it. "Consider" here is essentially a more thoughtful or formal way of saying "think of as," "view as," or "regard as."

Meaning 3 — To take something into account; to factor something in

In this sense, you "consider" something when you include it in your thinking or decision-making. It is about not ignoring or overlooking something important.

Examples:

  • "We need to consider the cost before proceeding."
  • "He made a decision without considering her feelings."
  • "Before you reply, consider how your words might affect him."
  • "The committee considered all the evidence before reaching a verdict."

The difference from Meaning 1 is subtle but real: Meaning 1 is about thinking over something broadly, while Meaning 3 is specifically about including something as a factor or piece of relevant information. In practice, these two senses often overlap.

"Consider" is a word with weight and thoughtfulness built into it. It suggests:

  • Deliberateness — you are not acting on impulse
  • Open-mindedness — you are genuinely engaging with the idea, not dismissing it
  • Responsibility — you are doing your mental duty before acting or judging

Compare these two sentences:

  • "Just think about it." — casual, light, no pressure
  • "Please consider it carefully." — more serious, implies genuine evaluation is needed

"Consider" also signals respect — for the idea, for the person presenting it, or for the decision at hand. This is why you often hear it in formal, professional, or serious contexts.
How to Use It in Sentences (Grammar)

Understanding the grammar of "consider" will help you use it naturally and correctly.

Pattern 1 — consider + noun/pronoun
The most common pattern.

  • "Consider the consequences."
  • "She considered his offer."

Pattern 2 — consider + -ing (gerund)
When a verb follows "consider," it must take the -ing form, never "to + verb."

  • ✅ "Are you considering leaving?"
  • ✅ "He considered calling her."
  • ❌ "He considered to call her." ← This is wrong.

Pattern 3 — consider + person/thing + noun or adjective (Meaning 2)

  • "I consider him a genius." (noun after him)
  • "She considers this plan perfect." (adjective after plan)
  • "They consider the matter closed." (adjective/past participle)

Pattern 4 — consider + whether / what / how / when…

  • "Consider whether this is the right time."
  • "We need to consider what we know."
  • "Consider how this will affect others."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Think about — informal and casual; no strong implication of thoroughness. "Think about it" is lighter than "consider it."

Ponder — deeper and slower than "consider"; suggests brooding or long reflection, often with some uncertainty or difficulty. You ponder when the question is really hard. You consider something before making a decision.

Contemplate — similar to "consider," but often more passive and philosophical. You contemplate life, fate, or abstract ideas. You consider a job offer, a proposal, or a problem.

Regard as / View as / See as — these are close to Meaning 2 of "consider," but "consider" carries slightly more weight and formality. Saying "I consider him brilliant" sounds more measured and deliberate than "I see him as brilliant."

Take into account — this is almost exactly Meaning 3 of "consider." These two phrases are nearly interchangeable: "Consider the weather" ≈ "Take the weather into account."

Deem — formal or official; used mostly in legal, academic, or bureaucratic writing. "The court deemed it lawful." In everyday speech, "consider" does the same job more naturally.

These are set phrases built around "consider" that you will encounter frequently.

"All things considered"
Meaning: After weighing everything; taking all factors into account.

  • "It wasn't a perfect trip, but all things considered, we had a great time."

"Consider yourself [something]"
Meaning: Treat yourself as that thing; act as if that is now your status.

  • "You passed the test. Consider yourself promoted."
  • "Consider yourself warned." (= I have now warned you; you cannot say I didn't)

"Under consideration"
Meaning: Currently being thought about or evaluated; not yet decided.

  • "Your application is under consideration."
  • "Several options are under consideration."

"On (further) consideration"
Meaning: After thinking about it (more carefully).

  • "On further consideration, I've decided to decline the offer."

"Give consideration to"
A more formal way of saying "consider." Common in official or professional writing.

  • "We will give serious consideration to your suggestion."

SenseWhat it meansExample
  • Sense 1 — Think carefully about something (before deciding): "Consider the risks."
  • Sense 2 — Hold an opinion; view/regard as: "I consider him reliable."
  • Sense 3 — Take something into account: "Consider her feelings too."

All three senses share a common thread: deliberate, careful mental attention. Whether you are thinking through a decision, forming a judgment, or making sure you haven't overlooked something important — "consider" always implies that the mind is at work, honestly and thoughtfully.
